title: Between two teachers
hookLine: Epictetus the freed slave, Seneca the rich courtier: one school, two lives

lines: ONE IN CHAINS, ONE IN A TOGA.
cards: Two men, decades apart, belonged to the same school of thought. One began life in chains. The other ended up in a senator's toga.
One owned almost nothing; the other owned so much that his enemies made it a weapon against him. This year has given about a hundred days to Epictetus and about ninety to Seneca.
Tomorrow opens the notebook of an emperor who learned from both. So today, the last day of Seneca's season, the two stand side by side.

teach.h: EPICTETUS: BORN A SLAVE, WROTE NOTHING.
teach.b: First, Epictetus. Ancient sources say he was born a slave in Hierapolis, in what's now Turkey, and that in Rome he belonged to Epaphroditus, a freed slave who served Nero. He was lame; the sources disagree about why.
Once freed, he taught philosophy until the emperor Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome, then taught in Nicopolis, in Greece, for the rest of his life. He wrote nothing.
His student Arrian took notes, and that's the handbook you read. Second, Seneca.
Born in Córdoba, in Spain, into a wealthy family: a senator, a well-known writer, exiled, recalled, tutor and adviser to Nero, and very rich.
He wrote shelves of books himself. Third, the overlap.

teach.h: SAME CITY, NO SIGN THEY MET.
teach.b: For a while both lived in Rome at the same time, both near Nero's court. There's no evidence they ever met, and nothing in what survives of Epictetus mentions Seneca by name. Fourth, one school, two voices.
Epictetus teaches from the front of the room: blunt, demanding, funny, sure. Some things are up to us, and some are not; learn the difference.
Seneca writes from the seat beside you, confessing, circling back, admitting he's still learning. Yet side by side, their lessons land on the same few things. What's truly ours is our judgment.
Time and life are on loan. Rehearse losing them, and you'll hold them better.
A slave and a millionaire, from opposite ends of Roman life, reached the same short list.
That doesn't prove the list. But it's worth noticing, and it's why both are worth keeping.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism today read Epictetus and Seneca side by side, turning to the handbook for its clear rules and to the letters for their companionship.

games.q: Domitian expels the philosophers from Rome. you're Epictetus, a freed man with a bad leg and no fortune. what do you do?
o: stop teaching and stay quietly in Rome.
move to Nicopolis in Greece and teach there.
write a book defending philosophy to the emperor.
games.why: he went to Nicopolis and taught for the rest of his life. the students kept coming, Arrian among them.

practice: Picture Epictetus at the front of a small room in Nicopolis, leaning on his stick, and let one thing he taught you this year come back. Then picture Seneca at his desk, writing to a friend, and find one thing from him.
Hold the two side by side for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Arrian. The student who took notes on Epictetus's teaching, since Epictetus himself wrote nothing: the source of the handbook you read. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a porch, a colonnade. The Painted Porch in Athens, where Zeno taught, gave the Stoics their name.

carryVoice: Your line: two teachers. The blunt one at the front, and the friend in the next seat. See you tomorrow.
